summary: The note compares dragon myths across cultures, based on a study by Dr. Miranda Kwan and Prof. Jacob Emery. East Asian dragons are benevolent, wise rain-bringers, while Western dragons are chaotic, evil foes to be slain; Norse and Persian traditions add their own variants. It also covers dragons in art, modern culture, and as a mirror of societal values and fears.
one_line: A comparative overview of dragon myths worldwide, contrasting benevolent Eastern and malevolent Western dragons, with art, modern media, and societal meaning.
key_facts: A comparative study of worldwide dragon myths was published on September 15, 2023, by ethnologist Dr. Miranda Kwan and folklorist Prof. Jacob Emery.
East Asian dragons, particularly in Chinese culture, are depicted as long, scaled, four-legged serpents embodying wisdom, strength, and the power to bring rain.
Chinese emperors were associated with dragons, whose divine authority symbolized the emperors' legitimacy.
Dr. Kwan's fieldwork in rural Chinese villages, on her latest expedition in spring 2024, uncovered many stories in which dragons were venerated.
The annual Dragon Boat Festival races boats adorned with dragon heads to appease river dragons.
In Japan, dragons are associated with water bodies and agriculture and seen as guardians of prosperity and good fortune.
Dr. Theo Andersen's work, released on October 20, 2023, examines medieval Christian symbolism in which dragons represented sin and the devil.
European dragons are large, winged, fire-breathing beasts, and the legend of Saint George and the Dragon is one of the most enduring tales of this tradition.
In Norse myth, Jörmungandr is a colossal sea serpent that encircles the earth, embodying unknown terrors like natural disasters.
In Persian folklore, the Azhdaha is a dragon representing chaos but also immense power that had to be respected, if not revered.
The International Symposium on Mythological Artforms, convened on August 11, 2024, displayed dragon-inspired works by celebrated artists.
Eastern art depicts dragons with meticulous detail and vibrant colors, while Western art highlights their fierceness and portrays epic battles with dragon slayers.
Elaina Voss's literary and film series "Dragonlore" had its latest installment released last November, showing the continued fascination with dragons.
Modern narratives often make dragons complex characters that defy the binary of good and evil.
